stories.headline: Update: Trump Says US Will End $4 Billion in Annual Military Aid to Israel by Year's End
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said on Election Day that the United States will end roughly $3.8 billion to $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel by the end of 2026. In a phone interview with Fox News as voting began, he said the aid was no longer needed and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had raised the idea. Trump said the two leaders had made a deal months ago.

The announcement came after military aid to Israel and campaign contributions from Israel's backers became a live issue in U.S. political debate. Some outlets described the move as an effort to blunt election-year criticism of Washington's support for its ally. Others noted how quickly the politics around Israel have shifted. Some conservative commentators said it remains to be seen whether the administration will follow through.

It is unclear how the cutoff would be carried out, since existing aid is governed by a multiyear memorandum of understanding and congressional appropriations. The statement also follows reports of tension between Trump and Netanyahu over the timing of renewed strikes on Iran. Neither the Israeli government nor the White House had provided detailed implementation plans at the time of publication.

stories.headline: Update: Voting Machine Failures in Westchester County Threaten Delays in Key New York House Race
stories.summary:
Voting machines in New York's Westchester County malfunctioned on Election Day, rejecting paper ballots across much of the county. The Westchester County Board of Elections said the problem involved the thickness of the paper ballots. Officials were scrambling to resolve the issue.

The county is home to a closely watched House race involving Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, one of the tightest contests of the cycle. Reports said the malfunctions could create bottlenecks and delay the count, and that the winner might not be known for days. Ballots that machines could not read were expected to be set aside for later counting.

The problem adds to a broader backdrop of election-administration disputes. The Justice Department deployed about 1,000 monitors to all 50 states for the first time, and a federal judge barred armed officers and anyone with arrest power from serving as monitors. Courts also rejected administration efforts to force California to set aside ballots. Control of the House could take days to settle, as in prior cycles.

stories.headline: Seven Flights Across Europe Searched After Suspected Bomb Threats
stories.summary:
Seven passenger planes across Europe were inspected after a series of suspected bomb threats, with no explosives found. Two Ryanair flights, from Dublin and Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome, and the Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian Air Force. Planes were also searched in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria, including a Ryanair flight from Manchester that landed in Murcia.

Officially there is no link between the incidents, but authorities from several countries are cooperating to assess whether it was a coordinated attempt to disrupt airspace. The UK government called the incidents malicious hoax threats. Aviation security expert Paul Mason said such threats do not happen frequently, and the spread across many airlines suggested a deliberate act.

Passengers described delays and evacuations. One passenger said she was told nothing during the flight and that the plane was surrounded by fire engines, police and a bomb squad after landing. Two flights bound for Warsaw were also affected, including one from London Heathrow. Poland's security services inspected aircraft from London and Copenhagen.

stories.headline: Tenerife Striker Jesus de Miguel Dies After On-Field Collision; Spanish Police Open Inquiry
stories.summary:
Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died at 30 after a serious collision during a Spanish second-division match against FC Andorra on Monday. He suffered head and chest injuries in a heavy collision with goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off. His condition was described as stable but serious on Monday and worsened on Tuesday morning, and he died at 07:00 GMT.

Reuters reported that Spanish police opened an investigation for possible involuntary manslaughter. Under Spanish law, any death deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry. Spanish media reported that De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated on the way to hospital.

Tenerife said it was heartbroken, and club president Felipe Minambres said players would need professional support. Andorra expressed shock and offered help. The match was abandoned with the score at 2-2 in stoppage time, and Owono deactivated his Instagram account.

stories.headline: Update: Polls Open Across the US on Midterm Election Day as Republicans Defend Slim Majorities
stories.summary:
Polls opened across the United States on Tuesday for the 2026 midterm elections, with the earliest East Coast locations opening at 5 a.m. ET and dozens more states opening by 7 a.m. ET. Polls in California and several other West Coast states open at 10 a.m. ET. The first polling places begin closing at 6 p.m. ET in parts of Kentucky and Indiana, while most states do not begin closing until 7 p.m. ET.

Republicans are defending narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress. President Donald Trump has predicted the GOP will hold the House and the Senate for the remaining two years of his term. Speaking to supporters at a rally in Kansas on Sunday night, he said, "We're going to win and let's make the next two years bigger and better and stronger than ever before."

Democrats are seeking to flip control of at least one chamber and have focused on the Senate in the final days of the campaign. Earlier coverage this week noted record early voting in Ohio and a closing campaign shaped by disputes over ballots and election administration. The new development today is that voting is now under way, and results will begin to arrive as polls close this evening.

The outcome will determine whether Trump faces a Congress controlled by the opposition for the second half of his term, with consequences for oversight, spending and legislation. Control of the Senate could also shape judicial and executive nominations. Close races in several battleground states may delay a final call on control of either chamber.

stories.headline: US Presses Venezuela to Free Remaining Political Prisoners as Rubio Meets Foreign Minister
stories.summary:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco on Monday and urged the release of the remaining political prisoners held in the country, the State Department said. The two also discussed reforms intended to lay the groundwork for free, fair and credible elections.

More than 1,000 political prisoners have been freed since US forces seized Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in a military raid on Caracas on 3 January and took him to New York, where he faces drug-trafficking and torture charges. The Venezuelan rights group Foro Penal says 322 people remain in detention, many of them arrested after the disputed 2024 presidential election. Delcy Rodriguez, Maduro's vice-president, was sworn in as interim president and has the backing of the Trump administration.

The State Department said it remains committed to Trump's three-phase plan of stabilisation, economic recovery and political reconciliation, and democratic transition. A week ago Rubio said Venezuela's election infrastructure must be replaced and that change must come quickly. Rodriguez has since said there will be elections under a renewed electoral authority but gave no date.

Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize winner who returned to Venezuela on 25 October after nearly a year in exile, has pushed for elections in 2027. Opposition parties have voiced impatience with the pace of reform.

stories.headline: Morocco Welcomes End of UN Western Sahara Mission After US-Russia Security Council Deadlock
stories.summary:
The UN Security Council failed on Friday to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as Minurso, after Russia vetoed a US-backed proposal. A rival Russian draft to extend the mission also failed to secure enough votes. Morocco has welcomed the end of the decades-long peacekeeping mission.

The outcome raises questions about the future of Africa's longest territorial dispute and the fragile 1991 ceasefire between Morocco, which claims Western Sahara, and the Polisario Front, which has fought for independence for more than 50 years. Minurso was established to monitor that ceasefire and organise a referendum that was scheduled for 1992 but never held, as the sides could not agree on who was eligible to vote.

Algeria, Polisario's main regional ally, hosts its leadership and thousands of Sahrawi refugees near Tindouf, and says its position rests on the right to self-determination. Morocco regards the territory as an integral part of its own and has offered an autonomy proposal since 2007. Relations between Morocco and Algeria remain tense, with the dispute at the centre of their rivalry.

stories.headline: Sweden's Caretaker Prime Minister Kristersson Gets New Mandate to Form Government
stories.summary:
Sweden's acting prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, received a fresh mandate on Tuesday to try to form a government. The move followed a parliamentary vote in which Center Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist failed to win the premiership, a result that had been widely expected.

The vote leaves Kristersson, who has been serving in a caretaker capacity, with another opportunity to assemble a governing majority. Ringqvist's failed bid underscores the difficulty of building a stable coalition in the Swedish parliament following the recent election.

What happens next depends on whether Kristersson can secure enough support in parliament to avoid a further failed vote.

stories.headline: Update: US and Iran Signal Willingness to Keep Talking as Pezeshkian Cites Expanded Authority
stories.summary:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government has been granted more authority by the country's supreme leader to pursue peace talks. The statement came as President Donald Trump hinted at progress in negotiations, according to Bloomberg.

The signals follow a period of renewed hostilities. The US struck Iran's Qeshm Island on the eve of the midterm elections, the first attacks in two months, and Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly held a tense call over the timing of renewed strikes.

The conflict has had wide economic effects. BBC reporting notes that 12 vessels were struck in a week, that UK diesel prices have reached a record average of 200.01p per litre, and that a US aircraft carrier has been kept at sea on one of the longest deployments ever. Gulf states have voiced fears of fiercer Iranian retaliation if Washington strikes again.

It is not yet clear what the expanded negotiating mandate means in practice, or whether either side will make concessions on core demands. BBC analysis asks whether either side has an exit strategy, noting that none of the choices facing Iran's leaders offers a clear path to victory.

stories.headline: Saudi Arabia's Asian Cup Postponed to Late 2027 After Houthi Attacks
stories.summary:
The Asian Football Confederation has postponed the 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia because of a series of deadly attacks on the kingdom. The 24-team tournament, originally set for January 7 to February 5, will now run from December 23, 2027 to January 21, 2028, pending approval from FIFA.

In October, a Houthi missile attack on Riyadh's airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. The AFC cited "substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions" arising from developments in the region.

Other events in Saudi Arabia have also been disrupted. The Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition in Riyadh was cancelled, and the Asian Tour indefinitely postponed its season-ending golf tournament, scheduled for November 18-21. A Saudi minister has vowed a "serious response" to the Houthi attacks on airports.

The delay tests the kingdom's ambitions to become a destination for major international sporting events, Bloomberg noted. It is the second consecutive Asian Cup to be postponed, after the 2023 edition was moved to 2024 and to Qatar because of the Covid pandemic.

stories.headline: Update: North Korea Denies Being Behind Record $6.3 Billion Binance Hack
stories.summary:
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the $6.3 billion hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, the largest in history. Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, called the allegations "absurd rhetoric" and a "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.

The FBI, the Secret Service and blockchain analysts have attributed the attack to the state-backed group TraderTraitor, also known as the Lazarus Group. The same unit was blamed for the then-record $1.5 billion hack of Bybit in 2025. The FBI has asked industry partners to help block transactions involving accounts linked to the group.

Binance said a net $4.72 billion has been withdrawn since transactions resumed on Sunday, which it called a relatively limited portion of its roughly $157 billion in total assets. A spokesperson said withdrawal levels are stabilising to what the company considers normal and expected.

North Korea has long been accused of using cybercrime to fund its sanctioned economy, and has consistently denied such claims.

stories.headline: US Seeks Deeper Ties With Myanmar's Military-Backed Government to Access Rare Earths
stories.summary:
The United States plans to deepen engagement with Myanmar's military-backed government, Bloomberg reported. The aim is to counter China's influence and gain access to the war-torn country's vast rare-earth deposits.

Rare earths are critical to electronics, electric vehicles and defense systems, and China dominates global supply and processing. Washington has been looking to diversify sources of the minerals.

Engaging a military-backed government is likely to draw scrutiny given Myanmar's ongoing conflict and its record on human rights. Critics of such outreach typically argue it can legitimize military rule, while proponents say strategic competition with Beijing justifies pragmatic engagement.

Details of the plan were limited in the available report, and further specifics on the form of engagement are expected.
